claim: ADAM10 acts as alpha-secretase of the Alzheimer's disease amyloid precursor protein.
source: One of the proteases is the a-disintegrin-and-metalloprotease 10 (ADAM10) which acts as alpha-secretase of the Alzheimer's disease amyloid precursor protein.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: ADAM10 is required for neuronal network functions in murine brain.
source: ADAM10 is also required for neuronal network functions in murine brain, but neuronal ADAM10 substrates are only partly known.
evidence: This statement is made in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: 91 mostly novel ADAM10 substrate candidates were identified using proteomic analysis of Adam10-deficient neurons.
source: With a proteomic analysis of Adam10-deficient neurons we identified 91, mostly novel ADAM10 substrate candidates, making ADAM10 a major protease for membrane proteins in the nervous system.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by the proteomic data presented in the results.

claim: Several novel ADAM10 substrates, including NrCAM, are involved in brain development.
source: Several novel substrates, including the neuronal cell adhesion protein NrCAM, are involved in brain development.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the proteomic identification and functional analysis.

claim: Mistargeted axons were detected in the olfactory bulb of conditional ADAM10-/- mice.
source: Indeed, we detected mistargeted axons in the olfactory bulb of conditional ADAM10-/- mice, which correlate with reduced cleavage of NrCAM, NCAM and other ADAM10 substrates.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by immunohistochemical data in the results.

claim: Mistargeted axons in the olfactory bulb correlate with reduced cleavage of NrCAM, NCAM and other ADAM10 substrates.
source: Indeed, we detected mistargeted axons in the olfactory bulb of conditional ADAM10-/- mice, which correlate with reduced cleavage of NrCAM, NCAM and other ADAM10 substrates.
evidence: This correlation is stated in the abstract and supported by the combined proteomic and histological data.

claim: Ectodomain shedding is a mechanism that shapes the cell surface by controlling the ectodomain length of cell surface membrane proteins.
source: This process, referred to as ectodomain shedding, is a mechanism that shapes the cell surface by controlling the ectodomain length of cell surface membrane proteins thus modulating their function (Weber and Saftig, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to prior work.

claim: Membrane-bound metalloproteases of the metzincin family have a key role in catalyzing ectodomain shedding of membrane proteins.
source: Membrane-bound metalloproteases of the metzincin family have a key role in catalyzing ectodomain shedding of membrane proteins, in particular members of the 'a disintegrin and metalloprotease' (ADAM) subfamily (Weber and Saftig, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to prior work.

claim: ADAM10 is a ubiquitously expressed type I membrane protein.
source: One of them is ADAM10, which is a ubiquitously expressed type I membrane protein whose active site is located within its ectodomain, well positioned to shed the ectodomains of its substrates (Weber and Saftig, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to prior work.

claim: The active site of ADAM10 is located within its ectodomain.
source: One of them is ADAM10, which is a ubiquitously expressed type I membrane protein whose active site is located within its ectodomain, well positioned to shed the ectodomains of its substrates (Weber and Saftig, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to prior work.

claim: The Notch receptor requires ADAM10-mediated shedding for its signaling during differentiation and development.
source: A key substrate for ADAM10 is the Notch receptor, which requires ADAM10-mediated shedding for its signaling during differentiation and development (Hartmann et al., 2002; Qi et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Constitutive ADAM10-deficient mice die at embryonic day 9.5.
source: Consequently, constitutive ADAM10-deficient mice die at embryonic day 9.5 most likely due to a loss of Notch signaling (Hartmann et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to prior work.

claim: The embryonic lethality of constitutive ADAM10-deficient mice is most likely due to a loss of Notch signaling.
source: Consequently, constitutive ADAM10-deficient mice die at embryonic day 9.5 most likely due to a loss of Notch signaling (Hartmann et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation and represents an inference from prior work.

claim: ADAM10 acts as the constitutive alpha-secretase for the amyloid precursor protein (APP).
source: Another major substrate of ADAM10 is the amyloid precursor protein (APP) for which ADAM10 acts as the constitutive alpha-secretase (Postina et al., 2004; Lammich et al., 1999; Kuhn et al., 2010; Jorissen et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: ADAM10 possesses the ability to prevent the generation of the pathogenic Aβ peptide in Alzheimer's disease.
source: and thus possesses the ability to prevent the generation of the pathogenic Aβ peptide in Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Lammich et al., 1999; Kuhn et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: ADAM10 is a major drug target for Alzheimer's disease.
source: This makes ADAM10 a major drug target for AD (Postina et al., 2004), and an activator of ADAM10 expression has been tested in a clinical trial for AD (Endres et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: An activator of ADAM10 expression has been tested in a clinical trial for Alzheimer's disease.
source: This makes ADAM10 a major drug target for AD (Postina et al., 2004), and an activator of ADAM10 expression has been tested in a clinical trial for AD (Endres et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to prior work.

claim: E-cadherin and CX3CL1 have been identified as ADAM10 substrates in different organs and tissues.
source: Besides Notch and APP, additional ADAM10 substrates, such as E-cadherin and CX3CL1, have been identified in different organs and tissues (Hundhausen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to prior work.

claim: Little is known about ADAM10 substrates in the central nervous system due to the embryonically lethal phenotype of constitutive ADAM10-deficient mice.
source: Given the embryonically lethal phenotype of constitutive ADAM10-deficient mice, little is known about ADAM10 substrates in the central nervous system (Hartmann et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: APP, Neuroligin-1, and N-Cadherin have been identified as ADAM10 substrates in the brain.
source: A few ADAM10 substrates have been identified in the brain. Some of them have neuronal and synaptic functions, such as APP (Ring et al., 2007; Weyer et al., 2011; 2014), Neuroligin-1 (Blundell et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2008) or N-Cadherin
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Conditional ADAM10-/- mice lacking ADAM10 expression in most neurons show epileptic seizures, learning deficits and an altered morphology of postsynaptic structures in the brain.
source: While these mice circumvent ADAM10 dependent embryonic lethality, they show epileptic seizures, learning deficits and an altered morphology of postsynaptic structures in the brain and die postnatally.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Conditional ADAM10-/- mice die postnatally.
source: While these mice circumvent ADAM10 dependent embryonic lethality, they show epileptic seizures, learning deficits and an altered morphology of postsynaptic structures in the brain and die postnatally.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: ADAM10 is essential for synaptic and neuronal network functions in the mouse brain.
source: This demonstrates that ADAM10 is essential for synaptic and neuronal network functions in the mouse brain (Jorissen et al., 2010; Prox et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: The known ADAM10 substrates only partly explain the phenotypes observed in conditional ADAM10-/- mice.
source: Yet, the known ADAM10 substrates only partly explain these phenotypes and more ADAM10 substrates are expected to exist in brain.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a rationale for the study.

claim: The SPECS method allows specific enrichment of cell-derived glycoproteins which would otherwise escape detection by mass spectrometry due to their low abundance.
source: SPECS allows specific enrichment of cell-derived glycoproteins which otherwise would escape detection by mass spectrometry due to their low abundance.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the methodology.

claim: 313 proteins annotated as glycoproteins were identified in the mass spectrometric analysis of the neuronal secretome.
source: Considering at least two unique peptides per protein and detection of the protein (protein group) in at least 4 out of 5 biological replicates the mass spectrometric analysis identified 313 proteins annotated as glycoproteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the proteomic analysis.

claim: The majority of peptides identified in the secretome matched to the extracellular domain, but not to the transmembrane or cytoplasmic domains.
source: The majority of peptides matched to the extracellular domain, but not to the transmembrane or cytoplasmic domains (data not shown), which demonstrates that we had detected the proteolytically released ectodomain and not the full-length membrane proteins in the neuronal secretome.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the proteomic analysis.

claim: The detection of peptides from extracellular domains demonstrates that proteolytically released ectodomains and not full-length membrane proteins were detected in the neuronal secretome.
source: The majority of peptides matched to the extracellular domain, but not to the transmembrane or cytoplasmic domains (data not shown), which demonstrates that we had detected the proteolytically released ectodomain and not the full-length membrane proteins in the neuronal secretome.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data stated in the results.

claim: The identified glycoproteins in the secretome comprised 113 secreted proteins and 200 membrane proteins.
source: These comprised 113 secreted proteins and 200 membrane proteins of which 108 had type I orientation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 108 of the 200 membrane proteins identified in the secretome had type I orientation.
source: These comprised 113 secreted proteins and 200 membrane proteins of which 108 had type I orientation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The levels of 91 glycoproteins were significantly reduced in the secretome upon Adam10 deletion (p-value cut off of 0.05).
source: Label-free-quantification of our mass spectrometric analysis revealed that the levels of 91 glycoproteins were significantly reduced in the secretome upon Adam10 deletion considering a p-value cut off of 0.05 based on 5 biological replicates (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1 – A10 knockout quantified secretome data set).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the quantitative proteomic analysis.

claim: 46 membrane proteins remain significantly reduced in the secretome upon Adam10 deletion when applying FDR-based multiple hypothesis testing (FDR = 0.1).
source: When applying false-discovery rate (FDR)-based multiple hypothesis testing according the method of Benjamini and Hochberg considering an FDR = 0.1 and all identified glycoproteins as hypotheses, 46 membrane proteins remain significantly reduced (Figure 1C and Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis of the proteomic data.

claim: Not a single glycoprotein was significantly increased in the secretome upon Adam10 deletion.
source: Surprisingly, not a single glycoprotein was significantly increased in the secretome upon Adam10 deletion.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the proteomic analysis.

claim: Among the 91 significantly changed glycoproteins, 78 were membrane proteins comprising 57 type-I, 6 GPI-anchored, 1 type-I/GPI-anchored, 5 polytopic and 9 type-II membrane proteins.
source: Among the 91 significantly changed glycoproteins we identified 78 membrane proteins comprising 57 type-I, 6 GPI-anchored, 1 type-I/GPI-anchored, 5 polytopic and 9 type-II membrane proteins which we considered as potential ADAM10 substrate candidates due to their membrane localization (Supplementary file 1 – A10 knockout quantified secretome dataset).
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the proteomic findings.

claim: Type-I membrane proteins were enriched to 70% among significantly reduced proteins upon Adam10 deletion compared to 39% in the total secretome.
source: Among the significantly reduced proteins upon Adam10 deletion, type-I membrane proteins were enriched to 70% compared to the total secretome that contains only 39% type-I membrane protein (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 90% of the 42 most significantly reduced glycoproteins upon Adam10 deletion possess a type-I orientation.
source: This enrichment of membrane proteins with a type-I orientation was even more pronounced when we assigned the topology to the 42 most significantly reduced glycoproteins upon Adam10 deletion in the secretome of which 90% possess a type-I orientation (Table 1)
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Table 1.

claim: Most previously identified ADAM10 substrates have a type I orientation.
source: which is in line with the observation that most previously identified ADAM10 substrates also have a type I orientation (Weber and Saftig, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation to prior work.

claim: Previously described ADAM10 substrates Neuroligin-1 (NLGN1), fractalkine (CX3CL1), and APP were identified among the ADAM10 substrate candidates.
source: Among all identified ADAM10 substrate candidates we found previously described ADAM10 substrates like Neuroligin-1 (NLGN1), fractalkine (CX3CL1) or the amyloid precursor protein (APP) (Figure 1C, yellow ring with green cross) which validated our experimental approach (Lammich et al., 1999; Kuhn et al., 2010; Hundhausen et al., 2003; Suzuki et al., 2012; Reiss et al., 2005; Colombo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The identification of previously known ADAM10 substrates validated the experimental approach.
source: Among all identified ADAM10 substrate candidates we found previously described ADAM10 substrates like Neuroligin-1 (NLGN1), fractalkine (CX3CL1) or the amyloid precursor protein (APP) (Figure 1C, yellow ring with green cross) which validated our experimental approach (Lammich et al., 1999; Kuhn et al., 2010; Hundhausen et al., 2003; Suzuki et al., 2012; Reiss et al., 2005; Colombo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results as validation of the methodology.

claim: The SPECS-based substrate identification was characterized by high sensitivity as even small reductions in total shedding were detected in ADAM10-/- cells.
source: Our SPECS-based substrate identification was characterized by high sensitivity as even small reductions in total shedding were detected in ADAM10-/- cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the sensitivity of the method.

claim: In neurons, APP is mostly shed by BACE1 and only to a low extent by ADAM10.
source: For example, in neurons APP is mostly shed by the aspartyl protease BACE1 and only to a low extent by ADAM10 (Colombo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation to prior work.

claim: A 20% reduction in APP shedding upon Adam10 deletion was clearly detected in the SPECS analysis.
source: Yet a 20% reduction in APP shedding upon Adam10 deletion was clearly detected in our SPECS analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the sensitivity of the method.

claim: Neuroligin-1 is an 'exclusive' ADAM10 substrate, as its shedding was nearly completely abolished upon ADAM10 deletion.
source: Interestingly, some substrates, such as Neuroligin-1 are 'exclusive' ADAM10 substrates, as their shedding was nearly completely abolished upon ADAM10 deletion.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the proteomic data.

claim: For substrates including APP and CHL1, shedding was only partly reduced in ADAM10-/- neurons, indicating that they are also substrates for other proteases.
source: However, for other substrates including APP and CHL1, shedding was only partly reduced in ADAM10-/- neurons, indicating that they are not only substrates for ADAM10, but also for other proteases.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the proteomic data.

claim: The list of identified ADAM10 substrate candidates comprises entire receptor families involved in synapse function and formation and axon targeting.
source: The list of identified ADAM10 substrate candidates comprises entire receptor families involved in synapse function and formation and axon targeting (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Shedding of PTPRU, PTPRG, PTPRK, PTPRS, PTPRT and PTPRD was reduced to 12%, 17%, 26%, 40%, 43% and 42% respectively upon Adam10 deletion.
source: In case of the receptor tyrosine phosphatase family shedding of PTPRU, PTPRG, PTPRK, PTPRS, PTPRT and PTPRD was reduced down to 12%, 17%, 26%, 40% and 43% and 42% respectively
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the proteomic data.

claim: Shedding of NLGN1, NLGN3 and NLGN4 was reduced to 17%, 38% and 56% respectively upon Adam10 deletion.
source: while shedding of NLGN1, NLGN3 and NLGN4 was reduced down to 17%, 38% and 56% in the Neuroligin family.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the proteomic data.

claim: NLGN2 shedding was not significantly affected upon ADAM10 knockout.
source: Interestingly, NLGN2 shedding was not significantly affected upon ADAM10 knockout.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the proteomic data.

claim: Presynaptic Neurexins 2 and 3 showed only a mild reduction in shedding upon ADAM10 deletion.
source: Presynaptic Neurexins 2 and 3, binding partners of Neuroligins, showed only a mild reduction in shedding upon ADAM10 deletion (Figure 1F) suggesting that ADAM10 plays only a minor role in their proteolytic processing.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the proteomic data.

claim: ADAM10 plays only a minor role in the proteolytic processing of Neurexins 2 and 3.
source: Presynaptic Neurexins 2 and 3, binding partners of Neuroligins, showed only a mild reduction in shedding upon ADAM10 deletion (Figure 1F) suggesting that ADAM10 plays only a minor role in their proteolytic processing.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the results based on the proteomic data.

claim: Ectodomain cleavage of SLITRK1 and SLITRK3 was strongly reduced upon Adam10 deletion.
source: Besides these families ectodomain cleavage of member 1 and 3 of the SLITRK family was strongly reduced (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the proteomic data.

claim: Ectodomain cleavage of Protocadherin 8 and 9 was reduced upon Adam10 deletion.
source: Ectodomain cleavage of Protocadherin 8 and 9, which have been proposed to play a role in synaptogenesis, was also reduced (Yasuda et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the proteomic data.

claim: Protocadherin 8 and 9 have been proposed to play a role in synaptogenesis.
source: Ectodomain cleavage of Protocadherin 8 and 9, which have been proposed to play a role in synaptogenesis, was also reduced (Yasuda et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation to prior work.

claim: The L1 family has been proposed to play a role in axon targeting and function.
source: The L1 family, which consists of NgCAM-related cell adhesion molecule (NRCAM), L1 cell adhesion molecule (L1), Close homologue to L1 (CHL1) and Neurofascin has been proposed to play a role in axon targeting and function.
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to prior knowledge.

claim: Shedding of NRCAM was strongly reduced to 33% upon Adam10 deletion.
source: We observed that shedding of NRCAM was strongly reduced down to 33%.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the proteomic data.

claim: Shedding of CHL1 was mildly reduced to 60% upon Adam10 deletion.
source: Shedding of CHL1 was mildly reduced down to 60%.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the proteomic data.

claim: L1 shedding was reduced to 64% upon Adam10 deletion.
source: L1 shedding was reduced down to 64% (Figure 1F), which is in agreement with their additional cleavage by the protease BACE1 (Kuhn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the proteomic data.

claim: The reduction of L1 shedding did not reach statistical significance.
source: However, the reduction of L1 shedding did just not reach statistical significance.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the statistical analysis.

claim: Neogenin (NEO1) ectodomain shedding was reduced upon Adam10 deletion.
source: Another axon targeting molecule whose ectodomain shedding was reduced upon Adam10 deletion was Neogenin (NEO1), which belongs to the DCC family.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the proteomic data.

claim: Adam10 deletion resulted in reduced ectodomain cleavage of CADM1, 3 and 4.
source: Adam10 deletion also resulted in reduced ectodomain cleavage of CADM1, 3 and 4 which are members of the Cellular adhesion molecule family that has been proposed to play a role in axon myelination (Maurel et al., 2007; Park et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the proteomic data.

claim: The Cellular adhesion molecule family has been proposed to play a role in axon myelination.
source: Adam10 deletion also resulted in reduced ectodomain cleavage of CADM1, 3 and 4 which are members of the Cellular adhesion molecule family that has been proposed to play a role in axon myelination (Maurel et al., 2007; Park et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to prior work.

claim: The Low density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) was identified as a substrate of ADAM10 whose ectodomain shedding was almost completely abolished.
source: Interestingly, we identified the Low density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) as a substrate of ADAM10 whose ectodomain shedding was almost completely abolished.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the proteomic data.

claim: Ectodomain shedding of the GPI-anchored membrane-tethered matrix metalloprotease 4 (MT4MMP/MMP17) depends to a great extent on ADAM10 activity.
source: Finally, our data revealed that ectodomain shedding of the GPI-anchored membrane-tethered matrix metalloprotease 4 (MT4MMP/MMP17) depends to a great extent on ADAM10 activity.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the proteomic data.

claim: Cre infection strongly reduced levels of immature and mature ADAM10 in the neuronal cell lysate.
source: First, we verified successful Adam10 deletion upon iCre expression by immunoblot (Figure 2A, ADAM10). Cre infection strongly reduced levels of immature and mature ADAM10 levels in the neuronal cell lysate.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Significantly reduced or almost abolished ectodomain levels confirmed ADAM10 cleavage of Neuroligin-1 (NLGN1) and N-Cadherin (CDH2).
source: Significantly reduced or almost abolished ectodomain levels confirmed ADAM10 cleavage of the previously described ADAM10 substrates Neuroligin-1 (NLGN1) and N-Cadherin (CDH2) and matched the results in the SPECS experiment (Figure 2B), while their full length levels were unchanged or slightly increased (Suzuki et al., 2012; Reiss et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Full length levels of NLGN1 and CDH2 were unchanged or slightly increased upon Adam10 deletion.
source: Significantly reduced or almost abolished ectodomain levels confirmed ADAM10 cleavage of the previously described ADAM10 substrates Neuroligin-1 (NLGN1) and N-Cadherin (CDH2) and matched the results in the SPECS experiment (Figure 2B), while their full length levels were unchanged or slightly increased (Suzuki et al., 2012; Reiss et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2.

claim: LDLR, MT4MMP, LRRC4B, NRCAM, NEO1 and CNTN2 were validated as novel ADAM10 substrate candidates by immunoblots.
source: The following novel ADAM10 substrate candidates were validated by immunoblots (Figure 2A): LDLR, MT4MMP, LRRC4B, NRCAM, NEO1 and CNTN2.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: For all validated novel substrates, ectodomain levels were reduced while full-length protein levels in the lysate were either unchanged or increased.
source: For all proteins ectodomain levels were reduced, while full-length protein levels in the lysate were either unchanged or increased.
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the immunoblot validation.

claim: The quantitative reductions of the ectodomain levels measured by immunoblots corresponded very well to the reductions measured by SPECS.
source: Importantly, the quantitative reductions of the ectodomain levels measured by immunoblots corresponded very well to the reductions measured by SPECS (Figure 2B), demonstrating the quantitative accuracy of SPECS.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The correspondence between immunoblot and SPECS measurements demonstrates the quantitative accuracy of SPECS.
source: Importantly, the quantitative reductions of the ectodomain levels measured by immunoblots corresponded very well to the reductions measured by SPECS (Figure 2B), demonstrating the quantitative accuracy of SPECS.
evidence: This is stated in the results as validation of the methodology.

claim: In ADAM10-/- neurons, L1 shedding was reduced by about 30%, both by SPECS and immunoblot.
source: Another protein, which was validated is L1 (Figure 2B). In ADAM10-/- neurons L1 shedding was reduced by about 30%, both by SPECS and immunoblot (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In neurons, L1 is predominantly cleaved by BACE1.
source: demonstrating that in neurons L1 is predominantly cleaved by a protease different from ADAM10. This is in line with previous reports demonstrating that L1 is mostly cleaved by BACE1 in neurons (Kuhn et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to prior work.

claim: L1 is mostly cleaved by ADAM10 in non-neuronal tissues and cell lines.
source: whereas it is mostly cleaved by ADAM10 in non-neuronal tissues and cell lines (Riedle et al., 2009; Gavert et al., 2007; Maretzky et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to prior work.

claim: Adam10 deletion strongly reduced CDH6 CTF formation with CDH6 full-length protein levels being unaltered.
source: Adam10 deletion strongly reduced CDH6 CTF formation with CDH6 full-length protein levels being unaltered (Figure 2A, CDH6), indicating that ADAM10 is required for CDH6 proteolysis.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ADAM10 is required for CDH6 proteolysis.
source: Adam10 deletion strongly reduced CDH6 CTF formation with CDH6 full-length protein levels being unaltered (Figure 2A, CDH6), indicating that ADAM10 is required for CDH6 proteolysis.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the results based on the immunoblot data.

claim: Increased full-length protein levels of DNER in the cell lysate upon Adam10 deletion indicates that DNER is cleaved by ADAM10.
source: In case of the Notch ligand Delta-Notch EGF receptor (DNER) we observed increased full-length protein levels in the cell lysate, which indicates that DNER is cleaved by ADAM10.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the immunoblot data.

claim: Upon Adam10 deletion, a strong reduction of fractalkine ectodomain levels was observed, which corresponded to the levels quantified with the SPECS method.
source: In case of fractalkine (CX3CL1) we confirmed its known cleavage by ADAM10 (Hundhausen et al., 2003) using a sandwich ELISA to detect soluble fractalkine in conditioned media of neurons. Upon Adam10 deletion, we observed a strong reduction of fractalkine ectodomain levels, which corresponded to our prior quantified levels with the SPECS method (Figure 2B, CX3CL1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: All membrane proteins analyzed by immunoblot could be validated as ADAM10 substrates.
source: Taken together, all membrane proteins analyzed by immunoblot could be validated as ADAM10 substrates.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the results based on the immunoblot validation.

claim: 432 glycoproteins were identified in the cellular glycoproteome analysis.
source: Using SPECS for labeling primary murine neurons, we identified 432 glycoproteins of which 37 were significantly changed upon Adam10 deletion considering a p-value of less than 0.05 based on 4 biological replicates (Figure 3B, C, Table 2, Supplementary file 2 – A10 knockout surfaceome dataset).
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the cellular glycoproteome analysis.

claim: 37 glycoproteins were significantly changed in the cellular glycoproteome upon Adam10 deletion (p-value < 0.05).
source: Using SPECS for labeling primary murine neurons, we identified 432 glycoproteins of which 37 were significantly changed upon Adam10 deletion considering a p-value of less than 0.05 based on 4 biological replicates (Figure 3B, C, Table 2, Supplementary file 2 – A10 knockout surfaceome dataset).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Of the 37 significantly changed proteins in the cellular glycoproteome, 5 showed reduced levels while 32 proteins had increased levels.
source: Of the 37 candidate proteins, 5 showed reduced levels, while 32 proteins had increased levels (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Table 2.

claim: 62% of the significantly changed proteins in the cellular glycoproteome possessed a type-I topology.
source: 62% of the significantly changed proteins possessed a type-I topology (Figure 3E) while 22% were polytopic proteins (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: 22% of the significantly changed proteins in the cellular glycoproteome were polytopic proteins.
source: 62% of the significantly changed proteins possessed a type-I topology (Figure 3E) while 22% were polytopic proteins (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Previously known substrates like APP, L1CAM and CX3CL1 were found among the significantly changed proteins in the cellular glycoproteome.
source: Among the significantly changed proteins we found previously known substrates like APP, L1CAM or CX3CL1 (Figure 3E) (Lammich et al., 1999; Kuhn et al., 2010; Hundhausen et al., 2003; Colombo et al., 2013; Maretzky et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Substrate candidates ISLR2, CNTN2 and Neurexin 3 were identified in both the secretome and cellular glycoproteome analyses.
source: Furthermore, we found substrate candidates that we had already identified in the secretome of ADAM10 knockout neurons like ISLR2, CNTN2 or Neurexin 3 (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: There was a small overlap of only 13 proteins between significantly changed glycoproteins in the secretome and significantly changed glycoproteins in neurons upon ADAM10 knockout.
source: The small overlap of only 13 proteins between significantly changed glycoproteins in the secretome and significantly changed glycoproteins in neurons upon ADAM10 knockout showed that ADAM10 cleavage regulated full-length protein levels only in a fraction of cases.
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the overlap between the two analyses.

claim: ADAM10 cleavage regulated full-length protein levels only in a fraction of cases.
source: The small overlap of only 13 proteins between significantly changed glycoproteins in the secretome and significantly changed glycoproteins in neurons upon ADAM10 knockout showed that ADAM10 cleavage regulated full-length protein levels only in a fraction of cases.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the results based on the overlap analysis.

claim: ADAM10 may regulate substrate function by cleavage mainly at the cell surface without affecting total full-length substrate levels.
source: Potentially, ADAM10 regulates substrate function by cleavage mainly at the cell surface without affecting total full-length substrate levels, which instead may be subject to lysosomal degradation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the results.

claim: SEZ6 ectodomain cleavage was almost abolished and its cellular levels were increased exclusively upon BACE1 inhibition.
source: SEZ6 ectodomain cleavage was almost abolished and its cellular levels were increased exclusively upon BACE1 inhibition with the validated inhibitor C3, which shows that SEZ6 ectodomain cleavage is predominantly cleaved by BACE1, in agreement with a previous study (Kuhn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4.

claim: SEZ6 ectodomain cleavage is predominantly cleaved by BACE1.
source: SEZ6 ectodomain cleavage was almost abolished and its cellular levels were increased exclusively upon BACE1 inhibition with the validated inhibitor C3, which shows that SEZ6 ectodomain cleavage is predominantly cleaved by BACE1, in agreement with a previous study (Kuhn et al., 2012).
